documents.title: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): a definition
documents.text:
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique that improves a language model's answers by first retrieving relevant passages from an external collection of documents and then giving those passages to the model as context for its answer. The model writes the response, but the facts come from the retrieved text.

## The two halves of RAG

A RAG system has two components:

- **A retriever**, which searches a document collection and returns the passages most relevant to the question. It can use keyword search, vector search over embeddings, or both.
- **A generator**, which is the language model. It receives the question and the retrieved passages and writes an answer grounded in them, ideally with citations.

## Why it exists

Language models store knowledge in their weights, which has three limits. The knowledge stops at the training cutoff. It cannot include private documents the model never saw. And when the model does not know something, it may produce a confident but wrong answer. Retrieval addresses all three by supplying current, specific source text at the moment of answering.

## RAG compared with a plain model

| Property | Plain language model | RAG system |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Knowledge source | Training data only | Training data plus your documents |
| Updating facts | Retrain or fine-tune | Re-index documents |
| Citations | Not available | Can point to retrieved passages |
| Private data | Not included | Included if indexed |
| Main failure mode | Fabricated facts | Retrieving the wrong passages |

## Where it is used

Common uses include customer support assistants that answer from a help center, internal search tools that answer questions over company documents, and research assistants that summarize a set of papers. In each case the value is the same: answers that can be traced back to a source the user can open and check.

## A one-line summary

RAG turns a closed-book exam into an open-book exam: the model still has to write the answer, but it gets to look things up first.

## What a RAG prompt looks like

A typical prompt has three parts. First comes an instruction, such as "Answer the question using only the sources below. Cite the source number after each sentence. If the sources do not contain the answer, say so." Then come the retrieved passages, each with a number and usually its document title. Last comes the user's question. The model reads all three and writes an answer with markers like [1] or [2] that point back to the passages.

## How much it helps

The size of the improvement depends on the questions and the documents. On question sets built from a team's own documentation, it is common to see the share of fully correct answers rise from well under half for a plain model to roughly three quarters or more with retrieval, mostly because the plain model simply does not have the facts. The gain is smallest for general knowledge questions the model already answers well, and largest for private, recent or highly specific facts.

documents.title: What is RAG in AI?
documents.text:
RAG is a popular term in artificial intelligence right now. It stands for retrieval-augmented generation. A lot of companies are using it, and you have probably heard about it if you follow AI news.

Basically, RAG is a way to make AI chatbots smarter. Normally a chatbot only knows what it learned during training. With RAG, it can look things up. This means it can give better answers about things it did not learn about before.

RAG is useful for many things. Businesses use it to build chatbots that know about their products. Schools use it to help students find information. Lawyers and doctors are starting to use it too, although they have to be careful.

There are many tools that help you build RAG systems. Some of them are free and open source, and some of them are paid services. You can also build your own if you know how to code, and there are many tutorials online that show you how.

RAG is not perfect. Sometimes it still gives wrong answers. It also needs good data to work well. If your documents are messy or out of date, the answers will not be very good. You also need to think about privacy if you use it with sensitive information.

Many people think RAG is the future of AI. It makes AI more useful and more trustworthy. As the technology improves, we will probably see it in more and more apps that we use every day, from search engines to email.

If you want to learn more about RAG, there are lots of articles and videos online. It is an exciting area and it is changing fast, so keep an eye on it.

documents.title: RAG in plain language
documents.text:
Imagine you ask a well-read friend a question about your apartment lease. They know a lot about leases in general, but they have never seen yours. A careful friend would ask to see the lease, find the clause that matters, and answer from it. Retrieval-augmented generation asks a language model to behave like that careful friend.

In a RAG system, your question does not go straight to the model. It goes to a search step first. The search step looks through a collection of documents, such as a help center, a set of policies or a product manual, and picks out the few passages that seem most relevant. Those passages are then pasted into the prompt along with your question and an instruction to answer only from them.

The model still does the writing. It reads the passages, decides which parts answer your question, and puts the answer in plain language. Because the passages are right there in the prompt, the model is much less likely to invent facts, and the system can show you which passages it used.

This design has a practical benefit for the people who run it. When a policy changes, they update the document in the collection, and the next answer reflects the change. Nobody has to retrain the model.

It also has a practical weakness. The answer can only be as good as the passages the search step finds. If the search picks the wrong part of the lease, the friend will give you a confident answer about the wrong clause. That is why teams that build RAG systems spend so much time on search quality.

documents.title: A short history of retrieval-augmented generation
documents.text:
The idea of combining search with text generation is older than the current wave of chat assistants. Question answering systems have long worked in two stages: find candidate passages, then extract or write an answer from them. Retrieval-augmented generation is the version of that design built around large language models.

Early systems retrieved passages with keyword search and used a model only to pick out an answer span. As language models became able to write fluent paragraphs, the second stage changed from extracting a span to generating a full answer, conditioned on the retrieved text.

The retrieval side changed too. Dense retrieval, which represents passages and questions as vectors and finds the nearest ones, became common because it matches meaning rather than exact words. Later, many teams found that combining dense retrieval with keyword search worked better than either alone, especially for names, codes and rare terms.

As models gained longer context windows, some predicted that retrieval would become unnecessary, since you could paste whole documents into the prompt. In practice retrieval has remained popular because document collections grow faster than context windows, long prompts are slow and costly, and models tend to use information in very long prompts less reliably than information in short ones.

Today the term RAG covers a wide family of systems, from a simple search-then-answer loop to multi-step pipelines that rewrite the question, search several times, rerank the results and check the answer against the sources. What they share is the core idea: look things up before you answer.

One lasting lesson from this history is that retrieval quality has always mattered more than the generator. Systems with a strong retriever and an ordinary model have tended to beat systems with a strong model and a weak retriever, because the model cannot use what it is never shown.

documents.title: RAG: key terms glossary
documents.text:
Retrieval-augmented generation comes with its own vocabulary. This glossary defines the terms you will meet most often.

**Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).** A method in which a system retrieves relevant documents for a question and passes them to a language model, which writes an answer based on them.

**Corpus.** The collection of documents the system can search, such as a help center, a wiki or a set of reports.

**Chunk.** A piece of a document, often a few hundred tokens long. Documents are split into chunks so that search can return focused passages that fit in a prompt.

**Embedding.** A list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text. Texts with similar meanings have embeddings that are close together.

**Vector index.** A data structure that stores embeddings and finds the nearest ones to a query quickly.

**Keyword search.** Search that matches words in the query to words in the documents, scored with a formula such as BM25.

**Hybrid search.** Combining keyword search and vector search, then merging the results.

**Reranker.** A second model that reads each retrieved chunk alongside the question and reorders the chunks by relevance.

**Top-k.** The number of chunks kept after retrieval and passed to the model, often between 3 and 10.

**Grounding.** Making sure the model's answer is supported by the retrieved text.

**Faithfulness.** A measure of whether each claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved passages.

**Context window.** The maximum amount of text a model can read at once, including the question, the instructions and the retrieved chunks.

**Hallucination.** A fluent statement that is not supported by the sources or by fact. Retrieval reduces it but does not remove it.

**Citation.** A marker in the answer, such as [2], that points to the retrieved passage supporting a sentence.

documents.title: Is RAG just search with extra steps?
documents.text:
A common reaction to retrieval-augmented generation is that it sounds like a search engine with a chatbot bolted on. That is not entirely wrong, but it misses what the generation step adds and what it costs.

A search engine returns documents. The user still has to open them, read them, and combine what they find. A RAG system does that last part for you. It reads the top passages, pulls out the parts that answer the question, reconciles small differences in wording, and writes one answer. For a question whose answer is spread across three help articles, that is a real saving.

The cost is a new kind of error. A search engine that returns the wrong document is easy to spot, because you can see the document. A RAG system that retrieves the wrong passage can still produce a fluent, confident answer. The error is hidden inside good prose. That is why well-built RAG systems show their sources, so the user can check the passages behind each sentence.

There is also a difference in what counts as success. For search, success is putting a relevant document near the top of the list. For RAG, a relevant passage in position eight may be useless if the model only pays attention to the first few. Retrieval has to be not just relevant but well ranked and compact.

So yes, RAG is search with extra steps. The extra steps make answers faster to use, and they make errors harder to see. Both facts should shape how you build and evaluate a system.

documents.title: RAG compared with search, chatbots and fine-tuned models
documents.text:
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a way of building AI systems that answer questions by first looking up relevant text and then asking a language model to write an answer from that text. It sits between a search engine and a plain chatbot. The table below compares it with the systems people usually confuse it with.

## How RAG compares

| System | Where the knowledge comes from | Can it cite sources? | How it stays current | Typical failure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Keyword search engine | An index of documents | Yes, it returns the documents | Re-index new documents | Returns pages, not answers |
| Plain chatbot (no retrieval) | Only what the model learned in training | No, not reliably | Retrain the model | Confident answers that are out of date or invented |
| Fine-tuned model | Training data plus the fine-tuning set | No, not reliably | Fine-tune again | Learns style well, facts less reliably |
| RAG system | Retrieved documents placed in the prompt | Yes, it can point to the passages it used | Add documents to the index | Wrong or missing passages lead to wrong answers |

## What makes RAG different

The key idea is that the model does not have to remember the facts. They are handed to it at question time. That has three practical effects:

1. **Freshness.** Adding a new document to the index makes it available immediately, without any training.
2. **Traceability.** Because the answer is built from specific passages, the system can show which ones it used.
3. **Control.** You decide which documents the model can see, which matters for private or regulated information.

## What RAG does not change

RAG does not make the language model smarter. If the retrieved passages are wrong, incomplete or contradictory, the answer will suffer. If the model ignores the passages, the answer may still be invented. Good RAG systems spend as much effort on retrieval and evaluation as on the model.

## A one-sentence definition

RAG is a pattern in which a system retrieves relevant passages from a collection of documents and gives them to a language model, which then writes an answer grounded in those passages.

## When people use it

Internal help desks, product documentation assistants, legal and policy lookup, customer support and research tools are common uses. In a survey of 140 teams building language model features that we ran last year, 61 percent said their main product used some form of retrieval.

documents.title: Explain RAG like I am new to AI
documents.text:
Imagine two students taking an exam. The first has to answer from memory. The second is allowed to bring a folder of notes, look up the right page for each question, and write an answer based on what the notes say. Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, turns an AI model into the second student.

## The memory-only student

A language model on its own is like the first student. It learned a huge amount during training, but its memory has limits. It may not know about things that happened after training. It may mix up details. And when it does not know something, it often guesses in a confident voice. People call those guesses hallucinations.

## The open-book student

A RAG system gives the model an open book. When you ask a question, the system first searches a collection of documents, such as company manuals, help articles or research notes. It picks out the few passages that look most relevant and places them in front of the model along with your question. The model then writes its answer using those passages.

## Why that helps

- The model can answer about documents it never saw in training, such as your company's internal policies.
- When the documents change, the answers change too. Nobody has to retrain the model.
- The system can show you which passages it used, so you can check the answer yourself.

## Where the analogy breaks down

An open-book student still has to find the right page. If the search step brings back the wrong passages, the model may give a wrong answer or say it does not know. And a student can still misread their notes. Models sometimes ignore the passages or blend them with what they remember.

## A tiny example

Question: "How many vacation days do new employees get?"

1. The system searches the employee handbook and finds the passage about vacation policy.
2. It gives the model the question plus that passage.
3. The model answers: "New employees get 15 vacation days per year, according to the handbook section on time off."

Without retrieval, the model would have to guess, because your company's handbook was never in its training data.

## The short version

RAG means: look it up first, then answer. That simple idea is behind many of the AI assistants that answer questions about specific documents.

documents.title: Retrieval-augmented generation: frequently asked questions
documents.text:
**What does RAG stand for?**
Retrieval-augmented generation. The "retrieval" part finds relevant text; the "generation" part is a language model writing an answer from it.

**Is RAG a model?**
No. It is a way of combining a search step with a language model. You can build a RAG system with many different models and many different search methods.

**What kinds of documents can a RAG system use?**
Anything that can be turned into text: web pages, PDFs, help articles, emails, tickets, transcripts and database records. Tables and images usually need extra processing.

**Does RAG stop hallucinations?**
It reduces them but does not remove them. A model can still ignore the retrieved text, misread it, or fill gaps with invented details. Evaluation and good prompts help.

**Do I need a vector database?**
Not necessarily. Many systems use embeddings and vector search, but keyword search such as BM25 works well for many collections, and hybrid systems use both.

**How is RAG different from fine-tuning?**
Fine-tuning changes the model's weights by training it on examples. RAG leaves the model unchanged and gives it information at question time. Fine-tuning is better at teaching style and format; RAG is better at supplying facts that change.

**How many documents does the model see?**
Usually a handful of short passages, often between 3 and 10, chosen from a much larger collection. Sending too many can confuse the model and costs more.

**Can a RAG system cite its sources?**
Yes. Because the passages are known, the system can ask the model to mark which passage supports each sentence, or show the passages next to the answer.

**Is RAG expensive?**
It adds the cost of indexing documents and running a search for every question, plus longer prompts. For most teams this is cheaper than retraining a model whenever information changes.

**Where does RAG struggle?**
Questions that need reasoning across many documents, questions whose answers are not written down anywhere, and collections with messy, duplicated or outdated documents.

documents.title: What RAG is not: five common misconceptions
documents.text:
Retrieval-augmented generation has become a popular way to build AI assistants, and with popularity come some persistent myths. Here are five we hear often, and what is actually true.

## Myth 1: RAG means the model has learned your documents

It has not. In a RAG system the model's weights do not change. Your documents sit in an index, and a few passages are pasted into the prompt for each question. Remove a document from the index and the system can no longer use it.

## Myth 2: RAG guarantees accurate answers

RAG gives the model better material, but the model can still go wrong. In one internal review of 400 answers from a support assistant, 7 percent contained a claim not supported by the retrieved passages, even though the right passage had been retrieved. Retrieval reduces errors; it does not remove them.

## Myth 3: You need embeddings and a vector database

Embedding-based search is common, but it is a choice, not a requirement. Keyword search works well for documents full of product names, codes and exact phrases. Many strong systems combine both and then rerank the results.

## Myth 4: More retrieved passages are always better

Adding passages raises the chance that the right one is included, but it also adds noise and cost. Models tend to pay less attention to passages buried in the middle of a long prompt. A small number of well-chosen passages often beats a large pile.

## Myth 5: RAG is just a search engine with a chatbot on top

Search is part of it, but the details matter: how documents are split into chunks, how queries are rewritten, how results are reranked, how the prompt is assembled and how answers are checked. Two systems built on the same search engine and the same model can perform very differently.

## So what is RAG?

RAG is a design pattern. A system retrieves relevant text from a collection and asks a language model to answer using that text, ideally citing which parts it used. It is useful when answers depend on information that is private, specialized or changes often. Its quality depends on every step, not only on the model.

documents.title: The parts of a RAG system, labeled
documents.text:
A retrieval-augmented generation system is easier to understand when you see it as a set of parts, each with one job. Here are the parts most systems have, in the order a question passes through them.

## The parts

1. **Document store.** The original documents: articles, manuals, tickets, notes. Usually kept as text with metadata such as title, date and source.
2. **Chunker.** Splits long documents into passages small enough to retrieve and fit into a prompt, often 200 to 500 words each, sometimes with a little overlap.
3. **Index.** A data structure that makes passages searchable. For keyword search it is an inverted index; for semantic search it holds an embedding vector per passage. Some systems keep both.
4. **Query processor.** Cleans up the user's question. It may rewrite it, expand abbreviations or split it into sub-questions.
5. **Retriever.** Searches the index and returns the passages that best match the question, typically the top 20 to 50 candidates.
6. **Reranker.** An optional, slower model that rescores the candidates and keeps the best few, often 3 to 8.
7. **Prompt builder.** Puts the instructions, the question and the selected passages into one prompt, usually numbering the passages so the model can cite them.
8. **Generator.** The language model that writes the answer.
9. **Post-processor.** Checks the answer: that citations point to real passages, that the format is right, and sometimes that each claim is supported.
10. **Logger and evaluator.** Records questions, passages and answers so the team can measure quality and find failures.

## Which parts matter most?

| Part | Effect on answer quality | Effort to improve |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chunker | High: bad chunks hide the answer | Low to medium |
| Retriever | High: the model cannot use what it never sees | Medium |
| Reranker | Medium to high | Medium |
| Prompt builder | Medium | Low |
| Generator | Medium | Swap or upgrade the model |
| Evaluator | Indirect but essential | Medium |

## A useful way to debug

When an answer is wrong, walk the parts in order. Was the answer in the document store? Did the chunker keep it in one piece? Did the retriever find it? Did the reranker keep it? Did the prompt include it? Did the model use it? Most failures turn out to be upstream of the model.

queries.query: How does a RAG pipeline work?

documents.title: How a RAG pipeline works, step by step
documents.text:
A RAG pipeline answers a question in two phases: an offline phase that prepares the documents, and an online phase that runs for each question.

## Offline: indexing

1. **Load documents.** Collect the source material, such as web pages, PDFs or database records, and convert it to plain text.
2. **Split into chunks.** Break each document into passages, typically 200 to 800 tokens with an overlap of 10 to 20 percent so that sentences at the edges are not lost.
3. **Embed.** Run each chunk through an embedding model to get a vector.
4. **Index.** Store the vectors in a vector index, and optionally build a keyword index over the same chunks.

## Online: answering

1. **Embed the question** with the same embedding model.
2. **Retrieve** the nearest chunks from the vector index, and optionally the best keyword matches.
3. **Merge and rerank** the candidates, keeping the top 3 to 10.
4. **Build the prompt** from an instruction, the question and the chosen chunks, each labeled with a number.
5. **Generate** the answer, asking the model to cite chunk numbers after each claim.
6. **Post-process**, for example by turning chunk numbers into links to the source documents.

## Typical settings

| Setting | Common range | Trade-off |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chunk size | 200 to 800 tokens | Small chunks are precise, large chunks keep context |
| Chunk overlap | 10 to 20 percent | More overlap means a larger index |
| Candidates retrieved | 20 to 50 | More candidates help the reranker but cost time |
| Chunks in the prompt (top-k) | 3 to 10 | More chunks raise recall but add noise and cost |

## Where latency goes

In a typical setup, generation dominates. Embedding the question and searching the index usually take tens of milliseconds, a reranker adds roughly 50 to 200 milliseconds, and generating a few hundred tokens takes one to several seconds depending on the model.

## The weakest link

Each step can fail on its own, and errors compound. A good pipeline logs the retrieved chunks for every question so that a bad answer can be traced to the step that caused it.

## A worked example

Suppose a user asks, "Can I return a product after 30 days?" The question is embedded, and the vector search returns 30 candidate chunks about returns, refunds and warranties. The keyword search returns 30 chunks containing "return" and "30 days". After merging, the reranker scores the combined list and keeps the top 5. The best chunk is the return policy section that says items can be returned within 45 days with a receipt. The prompt lists the five chunks as sources [1] to [5], and the model answers that returns are accepted up to 45 days with a receipt, citing [1]. If the policy changes to 60 days, the team edits the policy page, the ingestion job re-embeds that chunk, and the next answer reflects the change.

documents.title: How does RAG work?
documents.text:
RAG works by combining two things: retrieval and generation. First the system retrieves information, and then it generates an answer. That is why it is called retrieval-augmented generation.

When you ask a question, the system searches for information that is related to your question. It uses special technology to understand what you mean, not just the exact words you type. Then it takes the information it found and gives it to the AI model.

The AI model reads the information and writes an answer for you. Because it has the information right in front of it, the answer is usually more accurate than if the AI had to remember everything by itself.

To make this work, you need to prepare your documents first. This usually involves breaking them into smaller pieces and storing them in a special database. This database lets the system find the right pieces quickly when a question comes in.

There are many different ways to build a RAG system. Some are simple and some are very complicated. The best approach depends on what you are trying to do and how much data you have. Simple systems are a good place to start if you are new to this.

Overall, RAG is a clever way to make AI more useful. It lets AI answer questions about your own documents, and it helps reduce mistakes. If you are building an AI application, it is definitely worth learning about, and there are plenty of guides to help you get started on your first project.

Another thing to keep in mind is that the quality of your documents really matters. If your documents are old or confusing, the answers will be old or confusing too. Take some time to clean them up before you start, and you will get much better results.

documents.title: Chunking strategies for RAG
documents.text:
Chunking, the way you split documents into passages, has a large effect on retrieval quality and is often chosen without much thought. Here are the main options and when each one works.

**Fixed-size chunks.** Split every document into pieces of a set number of tokens, such as 400, with some overlap. It is simple and predictable, but it cuts through sentences, tables and sections without regard for meaning.

**Sentence or paragraph chunks.** Split on natural boundaries and group sentences until a size limit is reached. This keeps ideas together and usually retrieves better than fixed-size chunks for prose.

**Structure-aware chunks.** Use the document's own structure: headings, sections, list items and table rows. A chunk might be one section of a manual, with its heading attached. This works well for well-formatted documentation, where headings carry a lot of meaning.

**Hierarchical chunks.** Index small chunks for precise matching, but return the larger parent section to the model. This gives the retriever focused targets while giving the model enough context to answer.

A few practical guidelines help regardless of strategy:

- attach the document title and section heading to each chunk, since a passage often makes no sense without them
- keep tables intact or convert each row into a sentence, because a half table is worse than none
- remove boilerplate such as navigation menus and footers before chunking
- test two or three chunk sizes on real questions rather than guessing

There is no universally best chunk size. Short, factual questions favor small chunks. Questions that need explanation favor larger ones. If your users ask both kinds, hierarchical chunking is often the best compromise.

documents.title: Vector search, keyword search and hybrid retrieval
documents.text:
The retriever is the part of a RAG pipeline that decides what the model gets to read, so it is worth understanding the main approaches.

Keyword search scores documents by how often the query's words appear in them, adjusted for how rare those words are across the collection. BM25 is the standard formula. Keyword search is fast, needs no model, and is excellent at exact matches like error codes, part numbers and names. Its weakness is vocabulary mismatch: a question about "cancelling a subscription" may miss a page that only says "ending your plan".

Vector search embeds the question and every chunk as vectors and returns the chunks whose vectors are closest to the question's. It handles paraphrase and synonyms well, because similar meanings land close together. Its weaknesses are the mirror image of keyword search: it can miss exact identifiers and rare terms, and it can return passages that are about the right topic but do not contain the answer.

Hybrid retrieval runs both and merges the results. A common merging method is reciprocal rank fusion, which gives each document a score based on its rank in each list and adds the scores up. Hybrid retrieval is a popular default because it covers the weaknesses of each approach with the strengths of the other.

| Approach | Strengths | Weaknesses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Keyword (BM25) | Exact terms, no model needed, fast | Misses synonyms and paraphrase |
| Vector | Meaning and paraphrase | Misses rare terms, topic drift |
| Hybrid | Covers both | More moving parts to tune |

After retrieval, many systems add a reranker, a model that reads the question and each candidate passage together and scores relevance more precisely than either search method. Rerankers are slower, so they are applied only to the top few dozen candidates.

documents.title: Building your first RAG prototype in an afternoon
documents.text:
You can build a working RAG prototype in a few hours with ordinary tools. The goal of a first prototype is not quality but a loop you can measure and improve.

Start with a small, real document set, perhaps 50 to 200 pages that your users actually ask about. Convert them to plain text and split them into chunks of a few hundred words, keeping each chunk's title.

For retrieval, start with keyword search. It needs no model and gives you a baseline you can understand. Add vector search later, once you can measure whether it helps.

For the prompt, number each retrieved chunk and give the model a clear instruction: answer the question using only the numbered sources, cite the source number after each sentence, and say you do not know if the sources do not contain the answer. That last instruction matters more than people expect.

Then write down 20 to 30 real questions and, for each one, note which document holds the answer. Run the questions, read the answers, and check two things: did the right document appear in the retrieved chunks, and did the answer stick to it? This small test set will guide every later decision, from chunk size to whether you need a reranker.

Resist the urge to add features before you have this loop. Most of the gains in early RAG projects come from fixing the documents and the chunking, not from more sophisticated retrieval.

Once the loop works, improve one thing at a time and rerun the same questions after each change. Keep a simple spreadsheet with the date, the change and the two scores. After a week you will know which changes moved the numbers and which only felt like progress.

documents.title: Why RAG pipelines fail in production
documents.text:
A RAG demo on ten documents usually looks great. The same pipeline on ten thousand documents and real users often does not. The failures tend to fall into a handful of patterns.

The first is retrieval misses. The answer exists in the corpus, but the retriever does not bring it back, often because the user's wording differs from the document's, or because the relevant passage was split across two chunks.

The second is ranking problems. The right chunk is retrieved, but it lands below several plausible but unhelpful chunks, and the model builds its answer from those.

The third is conflicting sources. Old and new versions of a policy both live in the index, and the model blends them or picks the wrong one.

The fourth is answering anyway. When nothing relevant is retrieved, the model answers from its own memory instead of saying it does not know.

The fifth is lost structure. Tables, lists and headings were flattened during ingestion, so a chunk contains a row of numbers with no column names.

Each pattern has a matching fix: query rewriting or hybrid search for misses, a reranker for ranking, document versioning and freshness metadata for conflicts, an explicit refusal instruction and a relevance threshold for answering anyway, and structure-aware ingestion for lost structure. None of these fixes help if you cannot see which pattern you are facing, which is why logging the retrieved chunks for every question is the most valuable thing you can add to a production pipeline.

A useful habit is to label every failed answer with one of these five patterns when you review logs. After a few weeks the counts tell you where to invest. In many systems retrieval misses and ranking problems together account for most failures, which is why retrieval work usually pays off before prompt work.

documents.title: Indexing time and query time: the two halves of a RAG pipeline
documents.text:
A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline has two halves that run at different times. Indexing happens ahead of time, whenever documents are added or changed. Query time happens for every question. Keeping them separate in your head makes the whole pipeline easier to reason about.

## Indexing time

| Step | What happens | Typical choices |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Load | Read documents from their sources | Files, wikis, ticket systems, databases |
| Clean | Remove boilerplate, navigation, duplicates | Strip headers and footers, normalize whitespace |
| Chunk | Split into passages | 200 to 500 words, split at headings or paragraphs |
| Enrich | Attach metadata | Title, date, section, access permissions |
| Embed and index | Make passages searchable | Embedding vectors, keyword index, or both |

Indexing can be slow without hurting users, because it runs in the background. A collection of 50,000 pages might take an hour to index and only a few seconds to update when one page changes.

## Query time

| Step | What happens | Typical choices |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Understand the question | Clean or rewrite the query | Expand acronyms, add context from the conversation |
| Retrieve | Find candidate passages | Top 20 to 50 by vector or keyword score |
| Rerank | Rescore candidates | A cross-encoder or a small model; keep the top 3 to 8 |
| Build the prompt | Combine instructions, question and passages | Number passages; ask for citations |
| Generate | The model writes the answer | Low temperature for factual tasks |
| Check | Validate the answer | Citation checks, refusal when nothing relevant is found |

Query time has to be fast. Users typically expect an answer within a few seconds, so each step has a time budget.

## Where problems usually come from

In our experience reviewing failed answers, the cause splits roughly like this: about 40 percent came from indexing (bad chunking, missing or stale documents), about 35 percent from retrieval and reranking, and about 25 percent from the prompt or the model. That is why many teams improve answers more by fixing their documents and chunking than by switching models.

## A practical tip

Log the passages that were retrieved for every question. When an answer is wrong, the log tells you immediately whether the right passage was found. Without it, you are guessing.

documents.title: A worked example: one question through a RAG pipeline
documents.text:
Descriptions of retrieval-augmented generation can feel abstract. Here is a single question followed through a small RAG pipeline for a company's IT help center, with the actual intermediate results.

## The setup

- Collection: 1,200 help articles, split into 6,400 chunks of about 300 words.
- Retrieval: hybrid search (keyword plus embeddings), top 20 candidates.
- Reranking: a small reranking model keeps the top 4.
- Generation: a language model with instructions to answer only from the passages and cite them with [1], [2] and so on.

## Step 1: The question

A user types: "vpn keeps disconnecting on hotel wifi"

## Step 2: Query rewriting

The system rewrites it to a clearer search query: "VPN connection drops on public or hotel Wi-Fi networks, troubleshooting".

## Step 3: Retrieval

The top five of 20 candidates, with scores:

| Rank | Chunk | Score |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | VPN troubleshooting: connection drops | 0.82 |
| 2 | Using the VPN on public networks | 0.79 |
| 3 | Wi-Fi setup for laptops | 0.61 |
| 4 | VPN client installation | 0.58 |
| 5 | Travel checklist for employees | 0.55 |

## Step 4: Reranking

The reranker reorders the candidates and keeps four: "Using the VPN on public networks", "VPN troubleshooting: connection drops", "Travel checklist for employees", and "Wi-Fi setup for laptops". It moved the travel checklist up because that chunk mentions hotel captive portals.

## Step 5: The prompt

The prompt contains the instructions, the four passages numbered [1] to [4], and the original question.

## Step 6: The answer

"Hotel Wi-Fi often uses a login page that blocks the VPN until you sign in, so open a browser and complete the hotel login before connecting [1][3]. If the VPN still drops, switch the client to the TCP connection mode in its settings [2]. Restart the client after changing the mode [2]."

## Step 7: Checks

The system confirms that every citation number points to a real passage and that every sentence has a citation. Both checks pass, so the answer is shown with links to the passages.

## What this example shows

The final answer used three of the four passages. The installation article, retrieved in step 3, was correctly dropped by the reranker. Each step narrowed and improved what reached the model.

documents.title: Reranking: the step most RAG tutorials skip
documents.text:
Most beginner tutorials for retrieval-augmented generation have three steps: embed the question, fetch the nearest passages, and send them to the model. Production systems usually add a fourth step between fetching and generation: reranking. It is often the cheapest large improvement available.

## What reranking does

The first retrieval step is built for speed. It compares the question against thousands or millions of passages and returns, say, the top 50. To be fast, it uses a simple comparison, such as the distance between two embedding vectors or a keyword score.

A reranker then looks at each of those 50 candidates together with the question and gives each pair a more careful relevance score. Because it reads the question and passage together, it can notice things the first step misses, such as negation, specific numbers or which passage actually answers the question rather than just sharing words with it.

## How much it helps

In tests on an internal knowledge base of 9,000 passages and 300 labeled questions, adding a reranker changed the results like this:

| Setup | Correct passage in top 3 | Correct passage in top 1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Embedding search only | 64% | 41% |
| Keyword search only | 58% | 39% |
| Hybrid search | 71% | 47% |
| Hybrid search plus reranker | 83% | 66% |

The answers improved too. With the reranker, reviewers rated 78 percent of answers fully correct, up from 66 percent.

## The cost

Rerankers are slower than the first retrieval step, because they process each candidate separately. Reranking 50 candidates might add 100 to 300 milliseconds. Most teams accept that in exchange for better answers, and limit the number of candidates to keep latency down.

## Practical advice

- Retrieve more candidates than you need, then rerank and keep a few.
- Measure whether the right passage reaches the top few, not only the top 50.
- Try reranking before trying a larger language model. Better passages often matter more than a better writer.

documents.title: Prompt assembly in RAG: how retrieved text reaches the model
documents.text:
After a RAG system has found the right passages, it still has to present them to the language model. This step, prompt assembly, is easy to overlook, but small choices here change how often the model uses the passages and how well it cites them.

## What a RAG prompt usually contains

1. **Instructions.** What the model should do: answer the question using only the passages, cite them, and say so if the answer is not there.
2. **The passages.** Usually numbered, each with a title or source line.
3. **The question.** Often placed after the passages, sometimes repeated.
4. **Format rules.** For example, "cite with [1], [2]" or "answer in under 150 words".

## Choices that matter

**Numbering.** Numbered passages make citations possible. Without numbers, the model cannot point to a source in a way software can check.

**Order.** Models tend to pay more attention to the start and end of a long prompt than to the middle. Many teams put the most relevant passage first, or last, rather than in the middle.

**Length.** Each passage costs tokens. Sending eight 400-word passages is roughly 4,000 words before the question even starts. Trimming passages to the relevant paragraphs can improve both cost and quality.

**Repeating the task.** With long prompts, small models in particular may lose track of the instructions at the top. Restating the key instruction after the passages, such as "answer using only these sources and cite each sentence", often improves citation rates.

**What to do when nothing fits.** Tell the model explicitly that it may answer "I could not find this in the documents". Without permission to refuse, models often invent an answer.

## A small experiment

On a set of 200 questions, we compared two prompt layouts with the same passages and model:

| Layout | Answers with at least one citation | Answers judged faithful |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Instructions only at the top | 81% | 84% |
| Instructions at the top and a one-line reminder after the passages | 94% | 88% |

The reminder cost about 25 extra words per prompt.

## Context windows

Every model has a maximum context length. If the assembled prompt is longer than the window the system actually uses, the start or end may be cut off silently. Check the real token count of your longest prompts, not an estimate.

documents.title: How RAG works (simple)
documents.text:
How does RAG work? Here is a simple explanation of how RAG works. RAG is a way to make AI better at answering questions.

RAG works in steps. First, there is a question. Then, RAG finds information. Then, RAG uses the information to make an answer. That is how RAG works.

The first step is the question. Someone asks a question. The question can be about anything. RAG takes the question and gets ready to answer it.

The second step is finding information. RAG looks for information that can help answer the question. The information can come from many places. RAG finds the best information it can.

The third step is making the answer. RAG uses AI to make an answer. The AI looks at the question and the information, and then it writes an answer. The answer should be helpful.

RAG is useful because it helps AI give better answers. Without RAG, AI might not know the answer. With RAG, AI has more information, so it can give a better answer.

Many companies use RAG. They use RAG for chatbots, for search, and for many other things. RAG is becoming more popular every year.

If you want to use RAG, there are many ways to get started. You can read more articles about RAG, watch videos about RAG, or try building a simple RAG system yourself. Learning how RAG works is the first step.

To sum up, RAG works by taking a question, finding information, and making an answer. It is a simple idea, but it is very powerful. Now you know how RAG works!

More about how RAG works: RAG works with many kinds of information. RAG can work with documents, websites, and more. RAG can be fast or slow depending on how it is built. RAG can be simple or complex. There are many ways to build RAG, and each way works a little differently. The important thing is that RAG helps AI answer questions better.

documents.title: Forum thread: why does my RAG bot ignore the documents?
documents.text:
**Original post:** I built a small RAG bot over our team's documentation. Retrieval looks fine when I print the passages, but the bot often answers from general knowledge instead of our docs, and sometimes contradicts them. What am I missing?

**Reply 1:** What does your prompt say? If it just says "here is some context", the model treats it as optional. Tell it to answer only from the passages and to say when the answer is not there.

**Original poster:** Right now it is "Use the following context to answer the question", then the passages, then the question.

**Reply 2:** Try putting the question first, then the passages, then a short reminder at the end: "Answer only from the passages above and cite them like [1]." Small models forget instructions that come before a long block of text.

**Reply 3:** How many passages and how long? I once sent 15 passages of 500 words each. The model mostly used the first and last ones. Cutting to the top 5 after reranking fixed a lot of it.

**Original poster:** Eight passages, about 400 words each. I am using a small local model.

**Reply 4:** Check the context window. Some local runners default to a small window, a few thousand tokens. Eight 400-word passages plus instructions can go past that, and the start of the prompt, where your instructions are, gets cut off without any error. Set the context length explicitly.

**Original poster (update):** That was it, mostly. The runner was set to 4,096 tokens and my longest prompts were around 5,000. After raising the window and adding a reminder line after the passages, the bot cites the docs in almost every answer.

**Reply 5:** Good catch. Also worth logging which answers have no citations at all. Those are format failures, and you want to count them separately from "cited the wrong doc", because the fixes are different.

**Reply 6:** One more thing: lower the temperature for this kind of task. At high temperature small models wander off the passages more often.

**Original poster (final):** Summary for later readers: set the context window explicitly, put a short reminder after the passages, send fewer and better passages, lower the temperature, and track answers with no citations separately.

queries.query: Should I use RAG or fine-tuning?

documents.title: RAG vs fine-tuning: how to choose
documents.text:
Use RAG when the model needs access to specific, changing or private facts; use fine-tuning when the model needs to behave differently, such as following a format, adopting a tone or handling a narrow task more reliably. Many production systems use both.

## The core difference

RAG changes what the model sees at answer time. Fine-tuning changes the model itself. Facts placed in a prompt can be updated in minutes and cited. Facts trained into weights are hard to update and impossible to cite.

## Side by side

| Factor | RAG | Fine-tuning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Best for | Knowledge: facts, documents, policies | Behavior: format, style, task skill |
| Updating | Re-index changed documents | Retrain on new data |
| Citations | Yes, to retrieved passages | No |
| Upfront cost | Index and pipeline | Labeled data and training compute |
| Per-query cost | Extra tokens for retrieved text | Usually lower, shorter prompts |
| Latency | Adds a retrieval step | No extra step |
| Risk | Wrong passages retrieved | Outdated or mixed-up facts |

## A decision checklist

- Do the facts change more than a few times a year? Choose RAG.
- Do users need to verify answers against a source? Choose RAG.
- Is the problem that answers are in the wrong format or tone? Choose fine-tuning.
- Is a small model failing at a narrow, repetitive task, such as classifying tickets? Choose fine-tuning.
- Do you need both current facts and consistent behavior? Use both: fine-tune for behavior, retrieve for facts.

## What about long context?

A third option is to put whole documents into a long context window. For a handful of documents this is the simplest approach and works well. As the collection grows past what fits in one prompt, or as cost and latency start to matter, retrieval becomes necessary again.

## A common mistake

Teams sometimes fine-tune a model on their documents hoping it will memorize the facts. Results are usually disappointing: the model learns the style of the documents but still gets specific facts wrong, and every update means another training run. If the goal is accurate facts, start with retrieval.

## Combining the two

The combination is common in production for a simple reason: the two methods fix different problems. A typical pattern looks like this. First, build retrieval over the document set and measure answer quality. Then look at the failures. If most failures are wrong or missing facts, improve retrieval. If most failures are answers with the right facts in the wrong shape, such as too long, missing the required fields or written in the wrong tone, collect a few hundred examples of good answers and fine-tune for that behavior.

Teams that follow this order tend to spend less, because fine-tuning is applied only to a problem that retrieval cannot solve, and the training data can be drawn from real questions the system has already seen.

documents.title: RAG or fine-tuning: which is better?
documents.text:
One of the biggest debates in AI right now is RAG versus fine-tuning. Both are ways to customize an AI model for your needs, but they work in different ways. So which one should you choose?

RAG is great because it lets the AI look up information. This means you do not have to train the AI on your data. You just give it access to your documents and it can find what it needs. This is often easier and cheaper than training.

Fine-tuning is great because it teaches the AI new things. You give it examples and it learns from them. This can make the AI better at specific tasks. However, it can be expensive and it takes time and technical skill to do well.

Some people say RAG is better and some people say fine-tuning is better. The truth is that it depends on your situation. Both have pros and cons, and there is no one right answer for every project.

If you are just getting started, RAG is often a good choice because it is easier to set up. If you have a lot of data and a specific task, fine-tuning might be worth it. You can also try both and see which one works better for you.

The AI field is moving very fast, so the best choice today might be different tomorrow. New techniques come out all the time. Keep learning and experimenting, and do not be afraid to try new things. Talking to other people who have built similar systems can also help you decide.

In the end, the most important thing is to understand your own needs. Think about what your users want, how often your information changes, and what your budget is. Then pick the approach that fits best, and be ready to change course if it does not work out.

documents.title: Fine-tuning does not teach facts well
documents.text:
A recurring surprise for teams new to language models is that fine-tuning on a set of documents does not make the model reliably know what is in them. It is worth understanding why, because it is the main reason retrieval exists.

Fine-tuning adjusts a model's weights so that it is more likely to produce text like the training examples. With enough examples, the model picks up patterns: the vocabulary of a domain, the structure of a report, the tone of a support agent. Those patterns transfer well. Specific facts transfer poorly. A model fine-tuned on a product manual might learn to talk like the manual while still giving the wrong number for a warranty period, especially if that number appears only once.

Facts in weights also go stale. When the warranty period changes, the old number stays in the model until the next training run, and there is no easy way to tell which answers are affected.

Retrieval sidesteps both problems. The current warranty period sits in a document. The retriever finds it, the model reads it, and the answer cites it. When it changes, you edit the document.

This does not make fine-tuning useless. It is the right tool when the problem is behavior rather than knowledge: a model that ignores your output format, writes in the wrong register, or struggles with a narrow classification task. A small amount of well-chosen training data can fix those reliably.

The practical rule is simple: retrieve facts, fine-tune behavior. When a team says its fine-tuned model "doesn't know" something, the fix is usually retrieval, not more training.

documents.title: A cost comparison of RAG and fine-tuning
documents.text:
Cost is often the deciding factor between retrieval and fine-tuning, but the two have very different cost shapes, so a direct comparison needs some care.

Retrieval has low upfront cost and an ongoing per-query cost. You pay once to embed and index your documents, which is usually cheap, and then every question costs a little more than it would without retrieval, because the retrieved passages add input tokens. If each answer includes five passages of 300 tokens, that is 1,500 extra input tokens per question. You also run and maintain the index.

Fine-tuning has higher upfront cost and a lower per-query cost. You pay to prepare training data, which is often the most expensive part because it needs human effort, and then for the training run itself. After that, prompts can be shorter, because the behavior you trained no longer needs long instructions or examples. But each time the facts or requirements change, you pay the upfront cost again.

| Cost item | RAG | Fine-tuning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data preparation | Clean and chunk documents | Write or label training examples |
| One-time compute | Embedding the corpus | Training run |
| Per-query cost | Extra input tokens | Shorter prompts |
| Cost of an update | Re-embed changed documents | New training run |
| Maintenance | Index, ingestion pipeline | Evaluation and retraining |

As a rough rule, retrieval is cheaper when facts change often or the document set is large, and fine-tuning becomes attractive when you serve a very high volume of a narrow, stable task where shorter prompts add up. For most teams starting out, retrieval is the cheaper way to get a useful first version.

documents.title: When we switched from fine-tuning to RAG
documents.text:
Our team spent two months fine-tuning a small model on our internal knowledge base before switching to retrieval. Here is what happened, in case it saves someone else the time.

The goal was a support assistant that answered staff questions about internal tools and policies. We had about 3,000 pages of documentation, so we generated question and answer pairs from them and fine-tuned on those. The first results looked promising in demos. The model used our terminology and wrote answers in the right style.

The problems showed up in testing. On a set of 150 real questions from staff, the fine-tuned model gave a fully correct answer to fewer than half. It often mixed up details from similar policies, and it confidently cited version numbers that had changed months earlier. Worse, we could not tell which answers to trust, because the model gave no sources.

We then built a basic retrieval pipeline over the same documents, with keyword and vector search and the top six passages in the prompt. Without any fine-tuning, about three quarters of the answers to the same 150 questions were fully correct, and every answer linked to the passages it used, so staff could check them.

We kept a small fine-tune in the end, but for a different purpose: teaching the model to say "I could not find this in the documentation" instead of guessing. Retrieval handles the facts. The fine-tune handles the behavior. That split has held up well.

The lesson we took away was to start with retrieval and measure before training anything. Our two months of fine-tuning were not wasted, since we learned a lot about our data, but a week of retrieval work got us further. If we were starting again, we would build the retrieval pipeline and the test set in the first week and decide about fine-tuning only after reading a few hundred real answers.

documents.title: RAG, fine-tuning or long context?
documents.text:
There are three common ways to give a language model knowledge it did not learn in training. Each one fits a different situation.

**Long context.** Paste the relevant documents straight into the prompt. This is the simplest option and needs no extra infrastructure. It works well when the material is small, perhaps a few documents, and changes per task, such as summarizing a single contract. It becomes slow and expensive as the material grows, and models tend to make less use of information buried in the middle of a very long prompt.

**Retrieval.** Index a large document set and fetch only the relevant passages per question. This scales to large and changing collections and supports citations. Its weak point is the retriever itself: answers suffer when the right passage is not found.

**Fine-tuning.** Train the model on examples. This is the right choice for behavior, such as format, tone and narrow task skills, and a poor choice for facts that change or must be cited.

These options combine. A typical mature system fine-tunes a model for format and refusal behavior, retrieves passages from a large corpus, and uses a long context window to fit more retrieved passages or a whole document when a question needs it.

If you are deciding where to start, ask how much material there is and how often it changes. Small and per-task points to long context. Large or changing points to retrieval. If the problem is not missing knowledge but the wrong kind of output, consider fine-tuning.

Whichever you pick, measure it on real questions before you commit. The best option on paper is not always the best option for your documents and your users.

documents.title: Decision matrix: RAG, fine-tuning, or both
documents.text:
Teams often frame the choice as RAG or fine-tuning, but the two solve different problems. A quick way to decide is to list what you need and see which approach covers it.

## The matrix

| Need | RAG | Fine-tuning | Both |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Answers about facts that change weekly | Strong | Weak | Strong |
| Answers that cite their sources | Strong | Weak | Strong |
| Private documents the model never saw | Strong | Medium | Strong |
| A consistent tone or house style | Medium (via prompt) | Strong | Strong |
| A strict output format, such as JSON | Medium | Strong | Strong |
| Specialized vocabulary or jargon | Medium | Strong | Strong |
| Low cost per question | Medium (longer prompts) | Strong (shorter prompts) | Medium |
| Fast to update | Strong (re-index) | Weak (retrain) | Medium |
| Small team, no training infrastructure | Strong | Weak | Weak |

## Reading the matrix

If most of your needs are about knowledge, especially knowledge that changes or must be cited, start with RAG. If most are about behavior, such as tone, format or following a specific procedure, fine-tuning may be the better fit. If you need both, many teams start with RAG, then fine-tune the model to use retrieved passages better or to follow a format.

## A rule of thumb

Fine-tuning teaches a model how to answer. RAG gives it what to answer with.

## Common mistakes

- **Fine-tuning to add facts.** Models can absorb some facts from fine-tuning, but they recall them unreliably and cannot say where they came from. Updating them means training again.
- **Using RAG to fix style.** Long style instructions in every prompt are fragile and costly. A small fine-tune can be more reliable.
- **Skipping evaluation.** Both approaches need a test set. Without one, teams cannot tell whether a change helped.

## Cost and time

A basic RAG system can be running in days. A fine-tuning project needs data collection, training runs and evaluation, often weeks. Fine-tuned models can be cheaper per question, because their prompts are shorter, which matters at high volume. Many teams therefore prototype with RAG and fine-tune later, once they know exactly what they need.

documents.title: RAG versus fine-tuning on a support corpus: our numbers
documents.text:
We support a software product with about 3,000 help articles and a steady flow of customer questions. Last quarter we compared four approaches on the same set of 500 real customer questions, each with a reference answer written by a support specialist.

## Setups

1. **Base model, no retrieval.** A mid-sized open model with a short instruction prompt.
2. **Fine-tuned model, no retrieval.** The same model fine-tuned on 8,000 past question and answer pairs.
3. **RAG.** The base model with hybrid retrieval and reranking over the help articles, top 5 passages.
4. **RAG with a fine-tuned model.** The fine-tuned model from setup 2, plus the same retrieval as setup 3.

## Results

| Setup | Fully correct | Partly correct | Wrong or invented | Cites a source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Base model | 31% | 28% | 41% | 0% |
| Fine-tuned | 52% | 22% | 26% | 0% |
| RAG | 69% | 18% | 13% | 92% |
| RAG plus fine-tuned | 74% | 16% | 10% | 95% |

Answers were graded by two specialists who did not know which setup produced them. They agreed on 87 percent of grades and settled the rest by discussion.

## What we learned

- **Retrieval mattered most.** Moving from no retrieval to RAG cut wrong answers by about two thirds.
- **Fine-tuning helped, but mainly with tone and format.** The fine-tuned model sounded like our support team and followed our answer template, which customers liked. Its factual errors were mostly about features that had changed since the training data was collected.
- **Combining both gave a modest gain.** The fine-tuned model used retrieved passages slightly better and cited more consistently.
- **Freshness was the deciding factor.** We ship updates every two weeks. Fine-tuned facts went stale quickly; re-indexing articles took minutes.

## Our choice

We run RAG with the fine-tuned model in production, and re-train the fine-tune about twice a year for style. Facts come from retrieval only.

## Caveats

This is one product, one model family and one set of questions. Teams with stable knowledge, or with tasks that are mostly about format, may see the opposite.

documents.title: When fine-tuning beats RAG
documents.text:
Much of the advice about language models now says "start with RAG". That is reasonable for question answering over documents, but there are tasks where fine-tuning is the better tool, and RAG adds cost without much benefit.

## 1. The task is about form, not facts

Classifying support tickets, extracting fields from invoices, rewriting text into a house style, or producing strict JSON are all behaviors. The model needs to learn a pattern, not look up information. A few thousand labeled examples can teach that pattern reliably, and the prompt can stay short.

## 2. The knowledge is stable and narrow

If the facts the model needs change rarely and fit in a modest training set, such as a fixed medical coding scheme or the rules of a board game, fine-tuning can work well. There is little to gain from retrieval when the information never changes.

## 3. Latency and cost per call matter a lot

RAG adds a retrieval step and longer prompts. At very high volume, the extra tokens add up. A smaller fine-tuned model with a short prompt can be several times cheaper per call. For one classification task we measured an average prompt of 220 tokens for the fine-tuned model against 2,900 tokens for a RAG setup with five passages.

## 4. There are no good documents to retrieve

Retrieval only helps if the answers are written down somewhere. When the expertise lives in examples, such as past expert decisions, rather than in documents, fine-tuning on those examples may capture it better.

## 5. The model must reason in a specialized way

Some domains need a particular way of thinking through problems, such as following a regulatory checklist in order. Fine-tuning on worked examples can teach that procedure more reliably than instructions in a prompt.

## Where RAG still wins

Facts that change, documents that must be cited, private collections that cannot go into training data, and anything where users need to check the source. In those cases, fine-tuning alone is the wrong tool.

## The honest answer

The choice depends on whether your problem is mostly "what to say" or "how to say it". Many real systems need some of each, which is why combining the two is common.

documents.title: Combining RAG and fine-tuning in one system
documents.text:
RAG and fine-tuning are often presented as rivals, but many production systems use both. Each covers a weakness of the other. Here is how teams typically combine them, and what to watch out for.

## Pattern 1: Fine-tune the model to use retrieved passages

A general model given retrieved passages may ignore them, quote them too much or fail to cite them. Fine-tuning on examples that show a question, a set of passages and a good grounded answer teaches the model to read the passages, cite them and say "not found" when appropriate. This is sometimes called retrieval-aware fine-tuning.

## Pattern 2: Fine-tune for format, retrieve for facts

The model is fine-tuned to produce answers in a fixed structure, such as a summary, steps and a citation list, and in the organization's tone. All facts come from retrieval. Updating facts never requires retraining.

## Pattern 3: Fine-tune the retriever, not the generator

Sometimes the weak point is search, not writing. Training the embedding model or the reranker on your own questions and relevant passages can improve retrieval for specialized vocabulary. The generator can stay unchanged.

## Pattern 4: Route between them

Simple, stable questions, such as "what are your opening hours", go to a small fine-tuned model with no retrieval. Complex or fact-heavy questions go to the RAG pipeline. A lightweight classifier decides.

## Comparison of the patterns

| Pattern | Main benefit | Main cost | Good first step? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Retrieval-aware fine-tuning | Better grounding and citations | Needs grounded training examples | After RAG is working |
| Format fine-tuning | Consistent output | Retraining when the format changes | Yes, if format matters |
| Retriever fine-tuning | Better search in niche domains | Needs labeled question and passage pairs | When retrieval is the bottleneck |
| Routing | Lower cost | More moving parts | At high volume |

## Pitfalls

- Fine-tuning on answers that contain facts can make the model rely on memorized facts over retrieved ones. Keep factual content in the passages, not only in the training answers.
- Evaluate each part separately. If quality drops, you need to know whether retrieval or generation changed.
- Keep the training data current. A format fine-tune trained on outdated answers can carry old facts along with the style.
