documents.title: Questions to ask before choosing RAG or fine-tuning
documents.text:
Before committing to an approach, it helps to answer a short list of questions honestly. The answers usually make the choice obvious.

## About the information

1. **Where does the information live today?** If it is in documents, wikis or databases, RAG can use it directly. If it lives mainly in people's heads or in examples of past decisions, fine-tuning on those examples may capture it better.
2. **How often does it change?** Weekly or monthly changes point to RAG. Information that is stable for years can be trained in.
3. **Must answers show their sources?** If users, auditors or regulators need to check where an answer came from, RAG is close to required.
4. **Is any of it sensitive?** Training data can be hard to remove from a model later. With RAG, removing a document from the index removes it from answers.

## About the task

5. **Is the main problem what the model says, or how it says it?** Facts point to RAG; tone, format and procedure point to fine-tuning.
6. **How strict is the output format?** Rigid formats, such as fixed JSON schemas, are often easier to get reliably with fine-tuning.
7. **How long can a response take?** Retrieval adds latency, often a few hundred milliseconds. For most chat uses that is fine; for some real-time uses it is not.

## About the team

8. **Do you have labeled examples?** Fine-tuning needs hundreds to thousands of good examples. RAG needs good documents and a test set.
9. **Can you run training jobs?** Fine-tuning needs infrastructure, or a provider that offers it, and someone to evaluate each run.
10. **How will you measure success?** Either way, you need a test set of real questions with reference answers. Build it first.

## Scoring your answers

| Mostly yes to | Suggests |
| --- | --- |
| 1, 2, 3, 4 | RAG |
| 5 (how), 6, 8, 9 | Fine-tuning |
| A mix | Start with RAG, add fine-tuning for format later |

## The question people forget

What happens when the system does not know? A RAG system can be told to say "not found" when retrieval returns nothing useful. A fine-tuned model has no such signal and is more likely to guess. If wrong answers are costly, that difference alone may decide the matter.

queries.query: How do you evaluate a RAG system?

documents.title: How to evaluate a RAG system
documents.text:
Evaluate a RAG system in two layers: measure retrieval (did the system find the passages that contain the answer?) and measure generation (is the answer correct and supported by those passages?). Measuring them separately tells you which part to fix.

## Build a test set first

Collect 50 to 200 real questions. For each, record the document or passage that contains the answer and a short reference answer. Real user questions are better than invented ones, because they include the vague wording and typos your system will actually see.

## Retrieval metrics

| Metric | What it measures | How to compute |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Recall@k | Did the right passage appear in the top k? | Share of questions with a hit in the top k |
| Mean reciprocal rank | How high the first right passage ranks | Average of 1 / rank of the first hit |
| Precision@k | How much of the top k is relevant | Relevant passages in top k divided by k |

Recall@k is the most important for RAG, because a passage the model never sees cannot help the answer.

## Generation metrics

- **Faithfulness:** the share of claims in the answer that are supported by the retrieved passages.
- **Answer correctness:** whether the answer matches the reference answer.
- **Citation accuracy:** whether each cited passage actually supports the sentence it is attached to.
- **Refusal behavior:** whether the system says it does not know when the answer is not in the corpus. Include 10 to 20 percent of questions with no answer in the corpus to test this.

## Human and model judges

Human review is the most reliable but slow. Many teams use a second language model as a judge for faithfulness and correctness, then check a sample of its judgments by hand. In one internal comparison, a model judge agreed with human reviewers on about 85 percent of faithfulness calls, which is good enough for tracking trends but not for final sign-off.

## Track over time

Run the test set on every change to chunking, retrieval or prompts. A change that raises recall can lower faithfulness if it adds noisy passages, so watch both.

## A minimal evaluation routine

1. Run every question through the system and save the retrieved passages and the answer.
2. Compute recall@k from the saved passages and the labeled answer passages.
3. Score faithfulness and correctness for each answer, with a model judge or by hand.
4. Read the 10 worst answers in full, and label each one as a retrieval failure or a generation failure.
5. Fix the most common failure type and run the routine again.

This routine takes an hour or two for a test set of 100 questions, and it turns vague impressions of quality into numbers you can compare from one version to the next.

documents.title: Testing your RAG chatbot
documents.text:
Testing is an important part of building a RAG chatbot. You want to make sure your chatbot gives good answers before you launch it to your users.

The easiest way to test is to just ask it questions. Try asking it different things and see if the answers make sense. Ask your coworkers to try it too, because they might ask questions you did not think of. Write down any problems you find.

You should also check if the chatbot is making things up. Sometimes AI models give answers that sound right but are actually wrong. Compare the answers to your documents to make sure they are accurate.

There are also tools that can help you test your RAG system automatically. Some of them use AI to grade the answers. These can save you a lot of time, especially if you have a lot of questions to test. Some are free and some cost money.

It is also a good idea to get feedback from real users after you launch. Add a thumbs up and thumbs down button so users can tell you when an answer is good or bad. Use this feedback to improve your system over time.

Remember that testing is not a one-time thing. Every time you change your system, you should test it again. AI systems can be unpredictable, so it is better to be safe than sorry. With good testing, you can build a chatbot that your users will love and trust.

Finally, do not forget about speed. Even a correct answer is not very helpful if it takes too long to appear. Check how long your chatbot takes to answer, and try to keep it fast so users do not get frustrated and leave.

documents.title: Faithfulness: the metric that matters most
documents.text:
Of all the ways to measure a RAG system's answers, faithfulness tells you the most about whether the system can be trusted. An answer is faithful when every claim in it is supported by the passages the system retrieved.

Faithfulness is different from correctness. An answer can be correct but unfaithful, when the model answers from its own memory and happens to be right. It can also be faithful but incorrect, when the retrieved passage itself is out of date or wrong. Both matter, but they point to different fixes. Unfaithful answers mean the model is ignoring its sources, which calls for prompt changes, a stronger instruction to cite, or a different model. Faithful but wrong answers mean the documents or the retriever need attention.

Measuring faithfulness usually works claim by claim:

1. Split the answer into individual claims, typically one per sentence.
2. For each claim, check whether any retrieved passage supports it.
3. Report the share of supported claims, and flag answers with any unsupported claim.

A human can do this reliably for a few dozen answers. For larger test sets, teams often use a second model as the checker, with careful instructions and a sample of its judgments reviewed by a person.

Citations make faithfulness easier to check. If the answer cites passage numbers after each sentence, the checker only has to compare each sentence with the passages it cites, which is faster and more accurate than searching all retrieved passages. Citation accuracy, whether the cited passage really supports its sentence, is a useful metric in its own right.

documents.title: Building a RAG test set that reflects real users
documents.text:
Most RAG evaluations are only as good as their test set, and test sets are often the weakest part. A test set written by the team that built the system tends to use the same vocabulary as the documents, which makes retrieval look better than it is.

Start from real questions. Search logs, support tickets, chat transcripts and internal help channels are all good sources. Keep the original wording, including vague phrasing and spelling mistakes.

Label each question with the passage or passages that answer it. This is slow, but it is what lets you compute retrieval metrics. For questions that need several passages, record all of them.

Cover the hard cases deliberately:

- questions whose answers span two or more documents
- questions about recently changed information
- questions with similar but different answers in different documents
- questions whose answer is not in the corpus at all
- questions that use different words from the documents

Keep the test set fixed once you start comparing versions, and add to it in batches rather than editing it as you go. If you change the test set and the system at the same time, you cannot tell which change moved the numbers.

A test set of 100 well-chosen questions is usually more useful than 1,000 generated ones, because each question has been checked and each failure tells you something.

Finally, write down what a good answer looks like for each question, not just where the answer lives. A short reference answer makes it possible to judge correctness consistently, whether the judge is a person or a model, and it keeps different reviewers from applying different standards.

documents.title: Retrieval metrics explained with an example
documents.text:
Retrieval metrics can sound abstract, so here is a small worked example.

Suppose your test set has four questions, and for each one you know which passage contains the answer. The system retrieves five passages per question. The correct passage lands at these ranks:

| Question | Rank of correct passage | Hit in top 5? | Reciprocal rank |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 1 | Yes | 1.00 |
| B | 3 | Yes | 0.33 |
| C | Not retrieved | No | 0.00 |
| D | 2 | Yes | 0.50 |

**Recall@5** is the share of questions where the correct passage appears in the top five: 3 of 4, or 75 percent.

**Mean reciprocal rank (MRR)** averages one divided by the rank of the correct passage, counting a miss as zero: (1.00 + 0.33 + 0.00 + 0.50) / 4, or about 0.46.

Recall tells you whether the model had a chance to see the answer. MRR tells you how close to the top it was, which matters because models tend to rely more on passages near the start of the context.

In this example, question C is the most urgent problem: no prompt change can fix an answer the model never saw. Look at its wording and the document it should have matched. Often the cause is a vocabulary mismatch or a passage split across two chunks.

Once recall is high, work on MRR, for example by adding a reranker, so that the right passage tends to be first.

Note what these numbers do not tell you. Recall and MRR say nothing about whether the model used the passage correctly once it saw it. A system can have perfect recall and still write wrong answers, which is why retrieval metrics should always sit next to answer metrics such as faithfulness and correctness.

documents.title: Online evaluation: watching a RAG system after launch
documents.text:
Offline test sets tell you how a system performs on questions you chose. Once real users arrive, you need a second kind of evaluation that watches live traffic.

The simplest signal is explicit feedback, such as a thumbs up or down on each answer. It is useful but sparse, since most users never click, and it skews toward strong reactions. Treat it as a pointer to answers worth reading, not as a score.

Implicit signals fill in the gaps. Users who rephrase the same question right away were probably not helped by the first answer. Users who click a cited source and then ask again may have found the source did not say what the answer claimed. Users who escalate to a human after an answer are a clear sign of failure in support settings.

Log enough to diagnose each failure: the question, the retrieved passages and their scores, the prompt, the answer and the citations. Without the retrieved passages, a bad answer cannot be traced to retrieval or generation.

Sample answers for review every week. A small random sample, perhaps 50 answers, read by a person against the cited passages, catches problems that metrics miss, such as subtle misreadings and outdated documents.

Finally, feed what you learn back into the offline test set. Every real failure you find is a candidate question for the next round of testing, which keeps the test set close to what users actually ask.

Taken together, offline tests and online monitoring cover each other's blind spots: the test set gives you stable numbers for comparing versions, and live traffic shows you the questions you did not think to ask.

documents.title: A metric cheat sheet for RAG evaluation
documents.text:
Evaluating a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system means measuring two things separately: whether retrieval found the right passages, and whether the answer used them well. The table below lists the metrics most teams use, what each one tells you, and what it misses.

## Retrieval metrics

| Metric | What it measures | Needs | Misses |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Recall@k | Share of questions where a relevant passage is in the top k | Labeled relevant passages | Whether the passage was ranked high |
| Precision@k | Share of the top k that are relevant | Labeled relevant passages | Whether the single best passage is present |
| MRR | How high the first relevant passage ranks, on average | Labeled relevant passages | Everything after the first relevant passage |
| nDCG | Ranking quality with graded relevance | Graded labels | Easy to compute wrong; harder to explain |

## Answer metrics

| Metric | What it measures | Needs | Misses |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Faithfulness | Share of claims supported by the retrieved passages | A judge (human or model) | Whether the answer is correct if the passages are wrong |
| Answer correctness | Agreement with a reference answer | Reference answers | Answers that are right but phrased differently |
| Answer relevance | Whether the answer addresses the question | A judge | Factual accuracy |
| Citation accuracy | Share of citations that point to a passage supporting the sentence | A judge | Uncited claims |
| Format failure rate | Share of answers with no valid citation at all | A parser | Anything about content |
| Refusal accuracy | Whether the system says "not found" when it should | Questions with no answer in the corpus | Quality of answered questions |

## How to use them together

Start with recall@k. If the right passage is not retrieved, nothing downstream can fix it. Then look at faithfulness and correctness on the questions where retrieval succeeded. That separation tells you which half of the system to work on.

Count format failures separately from wrong answers. An answer with no citations at all usually means the model did not follow instructions, often because the prompt was too long or the instructions were unclear. That needs a prompt fix, not a retrieval fix.

## Baselines matter

Every number needs a comparison. If a system that cites every retrieved passage equally would score 0.2 on a share-of-citations metric, a result of 0.2 says nothing about your documents. Report the chance level next to the result.

## A minimum set

For a first evaluation, track recall@5, faithfulness, answer correctness and format failure rate on 100 to 200 real questions.

documents.title: Using a model as a judge: what can go wrong
documents.text:
Grading thousands of RAG answers by hand is slow, so many teams ask a language model to do it: given the question, the retrieved passages and the answer, decide whether the answer is faithful and correct. This works surprisingly well, but it has failure modes worth knowing before you trust the numbers.

## Known problems

**Position and length bias.** Judges often favor longer answers and, when comparing two answers, the one shown first. Randomize order and check whether scores track length.

**Self-preference.** A judge may rate answers written by a similar model more highly. Where possible, use a judge from a different model family than the generator.

**Leniency on unsupported claims.** Judges sometimes accept a plausible claim even when the passages do not support it, especially if the claim is common knowledge. Ask the judge to check each claim against a passage explicitly.

**Inconsistency.** The same answer can get different scores on different runs. Use a low temperature, a fixed prompt and, for important results, several judgments per answer.

**Prompt sensitivity.** Small wording changes in the judge's instructions can shift average scores by several points. Freeze the judge prompt and version it like code.

## Check the judge against people

Before relying on a judge, grade a sample by hand and compare. In one comparison on 300 answers, a model judge agreed with two human reviewers on 82 percent of faithfulness labels. The humans agreed with each other on 88 percent. Most disagreements involved answers that were partly supported.

| Label pair | Agreement |
| --- | --- |
| Human A and human B | 88% |
| Judge and human A | 83% |
| Judge and human B | 81% |

## Good practice

1. Keep a small, hand-graded set of answers and re-check the judge on it whenever the judge prompt or model changes.
2. Report judge scores with their sample size and, ideally, an interval.
3. Look at disagreements. They often reveal unclear guidelines rather than judge errors.
4. Do not let the judge be the only check on critical claims, such as prices, dosages or legal deadlines.

## When to skip the judge

For simple checks, use code. Whether every citation points to an existing passage, whether an answer has any citation at all, and whether it follows the format can all be checked exactly, with no judge needed.

documents.title: Our RAG evaluation dashboard, explained
documents.text:
Our team runs a RAG assistant for internal engineering documentation. About 2,000 people use it each week. Here is what our evaluation dashboard shows, and why each panel is there.

## Panel 1: Retrieval recall

The share of questions in our fixed test set (420 questions) where a relevant passage appears in the top 5. It is currently 87 percent. We look at this first, because a drop here explains most quality drops elsewhere.

## Panel 2: Faithfulness

The share of answer sentences supported by the retrieved passages, judged by a model and spot-checked by a person each week. Currently 91 percent. When it dips, the cause is usually a prompt change or a new model version.

## Panel 3: Format failures

The share of answers with no valid citation at all. We started tracking this separately after a model upgrade: answers looked fine, but 12 percent had dropped their citations. That would have been hidden inside the faithfulness score. It is now under 2 percent.

## Panel 4: Refusals

How often the assistant says it could not find an answer, split into correct refusals (questions we know have no answer in the docs) and incorrect ones. Too few correct refusals means it is guessing; too many incorrect ones means retrieval is missing things.

## Panel 5: User feedback

Thumbs up and down from real users, with comments. This is noisy, and only about 4 percent of answers get feedback, but it catches problems our test set does not cover.

## Panel 6: Cost and latency

Median and slowest response times, and average tokens per question. Retrieval changes that add passages show up here immediately.

## Weekly numbers (last four weeks)

| Week | Recall@5 | Faithfulness | Format failures | Thumbs up share |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 85% | 90% | 2.4% | 71% |
| 2 | 86% | 91% | 1.9% | 73% |
| 3 | 87% | 89% | 1.8% | 70% |
| 4 | 87% | 91% | 1.6% | 74% |

## What we learned building it

Separate metrics beat one combined score. Each panel points to a different part of the system, so a change in one tells us where to look.

documents.title: Golden test sets for RAG: how many questions do you need?
documents.text:
A golden test set is a fixed list of questions with known good answers, and often the passages that support them. It is the foundation of RAG evaluation. A common question is how big it needs to be.

## It depends on the size of the change you want to detect

With a small test set, random variation hides real changes. The table below shows roughly how wide a 95 percent interval is for a measured rate near 80 percent, at different test set sizes.

| Questions in the test set | Approximate 95% interval around 80% |
| --- | --- |
| 25 | 61% to 91% |
| 50 | 67% to 89% |
| 100 | 71% to 87% |
| 200 | 74% to 85% |
| 500 | 76% to 83% |

With 50 questions, a system scoring 80 percent could plausibly be anywhere from the high 60s to the high 80s. You would not be able to tell a 5 point improvement from noise.

## Paired comparisons help

When comparing two versions of a system on the same questions, a paired test, which looks at how each question changed, is much more sensitive than comparing two overall rates. Even so, with very few questions no test can show a reliable difference. With 4 questions, for example, the smallest possible two-sided p-value from an exact sign-flip test is 0.125.

## Practical sizes

- **Smoke test:** 20 to 30 questions, run on every change, to catch obvious breakage.
- **Regular evaluation:** 150 to 300 questions, run before releases.
- **Decision-grade comparison:** 500 or more, or repeated runs on a smaller set, when choosing between models or architectures.

## What goes into the set

- Real user questions, not only ones written by the team.
- Questions across all major topics and document types.
- Hard cases: ambiguous questions, multi-part questions, and questions with no answer in the corpus.
- A note of which passage supports each answer, so retrieval can be checked separately.

## Keep it fixed, then refresh it

Change the test set only on purpose, and version it. Results on different sets cannot be compared. Every few months, add new real questions so the set reflects how people actually use the system.

In summary, evaluating RAG is very important. There are many ways to evaluate RAG, including asking questions, using metrics, asking people, and using AI. Evaluate RAG often and keep track of your results. Good luck with evaluating RAG!

documents.title: Regression testing a RAG system before every release
documents.text:
RAG systems change in many small ways: new documents, a new chunking rule, a prompt tweak, a model upgrade. Any of these can quietly make answers worse. A regression test suite catches that before users do. Here is the routine we follow before every release.

## The steps

1. **Freeze the inputs.** Use a fixed, versioned test set of questions, and record the exact index version, prompt version and model version for the run.
2. **Run retrieval alone.** For each question, check whether a known relevant passage is in the top k. Compare recall@5 with the last release. A drop of more than 2 points blocks the release until explained.
3. **Run the full pipeline.** Generate answers for every question with the same settings as production, including temperature and context length.
4. **Run exact checks.** Every answer must have at least one citation, every citation must point to a passage in the prompt, and answers must follow the required format. Count format failures separately.
5. **Run judged checks.** Use a model judge, calibrated against human grades, to score faithfulness and correctness.
6. **Compare paired results.** For each question, compare the new answer's scores with the old one's. Look at the questions that got worse, not only at the averages.
7. **Read a sample.** A person reads 20 answers that changed the most. Numbers miss things that a reader notices immediately.
8. **Record the results** with the versions from step 1, so future runs can be compared.

## Thresholds we use

| Check | Blocks the release if |
| --- | --- |
| Recall@5 | Drops more than 2 points |
| Format failures | Rise above 3% |
| Faithfulness | Drops more than 2 points |
| Correctness | Drops more than 3 points |
| Latency (median) | Rises more than 20% |

## Things that caught us out

- A model upgrade that looked better on averages but stopped citing in 9 percent of answers. Step 4 caught it.
- A new document import that duplicated 600 pages. Recall stayed flat, but answers started citing outdated copies. Step 7 caught it.
- A context length setting that silently fell back to a smaller default after an update, truncating long prompts. Answers lost their instructions. We now log the prompt length and the configured context window for every run.

## How long it takes

On 300 questions, the full suite runs in about 40 minutes and costs little compared with a bad release.
